b.x: This is education, not a diagnosis and not an order. A daily medicine is not stopped on your own. Weakness on one side and slurred speech is care, and the stroke guide is on this site. This page does not dial.
Dignity comes first

An older person is not a burden. They are someone with experience, wisdom, and a will of their own. Always ask. Never decide for them without listening. Even in chaos, respect builds trust, and trust builds cooperation.
The pace is the slowest person's
It does not help that you are fast if the person you protect is left behind. The pace is theirs. If you need to stop, stop. If you need to rest, rest. Hurry kills more than the danger.
The needs are not yours

The heart is more fragile: less effort, more frequent stops. The medicine can be vital: it is not forgotten. The bone breaks more easily: a fall can be fatal. There may be confusion or fear: calm and routine are the shield.
The caregiver's kit

Beyond the basic kit, take heart, blood pressure, and diabetes medicines in the original box, with the name and the dose, and a list that can be read in the dark. A card in the pocket or on the neck: name, age, contact, conditions, allergies, and medicines. Shoes already worn, a firm sole, no heel. Clothes in thin layers: an older person feels the cold more, and a layer also eases the heat. Water in small, frequent sips. Thirst fades. The need does not. Soft food: dried fruit, a soft biscuit, a packed purée. A place to sit, a folding chair or a cloth, so they are not left standing. A soft light and a small lamp. A hard light bothers. Darkness increases fear and falls. Something familiar: a cloth, a photo, a rosary, a watch. In chaos, the known calms more than a speech.
The way

Choose the flattest way, not the fastest one on the map. Avoid stairs and uneven ground. If there is no other way, one step at a time. Never leave them alone, not even for two minutes. Confusion, fear, or losing the way can happen in an instant. Walk beside them, never ahead. Stay on the side of the heart or on the weaker side. You are the visual support and the support of the arm.
Time and the stop

Plan twice the time you would take alone. Stop every thirty or forty-five minutes, for five to ten minutes: breathe, a sip of water, sit. Panting, cold sweat, chest pain, or dizziness: stop at once and do not go on.
What is not ignored

Sudden confusion, not knowing where they are: it can be thirst, fatigue, or stress. Sit, water a little at a time, a calm voice. Short breath and chest pain: stop, sit, do not lie fully flat. Sudden weakness on one side of the body, slurred speech: that is a stroke. Do not move them much. Shelter them, keep them warm and calm, and get care. This page does not dial. Fever, confusion, and dark urine: thirst or an infection. Water a little at a time, a cool shelter, a close watch. A fall, even when they say they are fine: the fracture may not show at once. Do not make them stand up in one move. If there is pain, do not move them.
The medicine

Take more than you expect to need. If the crisis lasts, it cannot run out. Separate it by hour: morning, afternoon, and night, in a bag or a box. Do not stop blood pressure, heart, or diabetes medicine on your own. The lack can be more dangerous than the crisis itself. Keep it away from heat and damp. The plan for the pill is the doctor's, not this page's.
Fear and confusion

Speak with a calm, low voice. Do not shout. Do not rush. Repeat with patience: stress makes understanding harder. Explain before you do it. We will walk ten more minutes and then we sit. Keep a simple routine: a time to rest, to eat, to drink water. What can be predicted becomes safety.
They are not a child

You are not caring for a child. You are caring for someone who has lived longer than you. Ask: can you hold this? Instead of taking it from the hand. Ask for an opinion: which way do you think we should go? Even if the final decision is yours, the person stays part of it. Do not say do not do that. Say: let us do it this way, it is safer for both of us.
If they can no longer walk

Do not force it. Forcing can cause a faint or a serious heart problem. Find a safe shelter first. It is better to stay in a protected place than to risk the health on the way. A chair with wheels, a blanket as support, or a support improvised with branches and cloth, if the ground allows and there is someone to help. Do not drag the person.
If danger arrives and they cannot run

Stand between them and the danger. Your body is the first barrier. Keep them low and protected behind some cover. Leave only when the way is safe. Running with an older person is a fall and an injury.
The last word

Real strength is not in carrying other people in your arms. It is in walking beside them, holding the hand, and saying: do not be afraid, we go together, and we will arrive together. That is not weakness. It is humanity. And in the middle of chaos, humanity is what justifies survival.
